title: Emergency Vet Costs in Canada: What Dog Owners Should Know Before a Crisis
excerpt: Emergency vet care in Canada can cost hundreds or thousands of dollars. Learn what affects the bill, warning signs to watch for, and how to prepare before a crisis.
description: Emergency vet care in Canada can cost hundreds or thousands of dollars. Learn what affects the bill, warning signs to watch for, and how to prepare before a crisis.
body:
An emergency vet visit in Canada can start with a few hundred dollars and climb into the thousands before you have had time to think clearly.

When your dog is hurt, struggling to breathe, vomiting repeatedly, suddenly weak, in severe pain, or exposed to something toxic, you are not calmly comparing prices. You are trying to get help quickly.

That is why the real cost of emergency vet care is not only the final invoice. It is also the stress of making fast decisions, the fear of delaying treatment, and the pressure of figuring out what to do while your dog needs care now.

This guide is designed to help Canadian dog owners understand what emergency care may involve and make a practical plan before an emergency happens.

How much does emergency vet care cost in Canada?

Emergency vet costs vary widely depending on your location, the clinic, your dog's condition, and the level of care required.

As a general planning range, Canadian dog owners should expect emergency care to start in the low hundreds and potentially rise into the thousands if diagnostics, hospitalization, or surgery are needed. For example, an Ontario emergency animal hospital intake form lists an emergency examination and consultation fee of $268.31 plus HST before treatment, while other clinics may publish different fees or provide estimates only after triage.

Emergency vet serviceTypical planning range
Emergency consultation or exam$150-$300+
X-rays, ultrasound, or diagnostic imaging$300-$1,200+
Bloodwork, urine testing, or lab work$150-$600+
Overnight hospitalization$500-$1,000+ per night
Emergency surgery$1,500-$5,000+

These are planning ranges, not guaranteed prices. Costs can be higher in larger cities such as Toronto, Vancouver, Calgary, and Ottawa, especially when care involves 24-hour staffing, advanced imaging, intensive monitoring, or specialist support.

The best way to understand local pricing is to call nearby emergency clinics before you need them and ask how they handle exams, estimates, deposits, and payment expectations.

Why emergency vet bills can add up quickly

Emergency care is different from a routine vet visit. The team may need to assess your dog immediately, stabilize them, run diagnostics, monitor their condition, and prepare a treatment plan in a short period of time.

The final cost may depend on:

  • The seriousness of the emergency.
  • Whether your dog needs imaging, bloodwork, medication, IV fluids, oxygen, or pain control.
  • Whether your dog needs to stay overnight.
  • Whether surgery or specialist care is required.
  • Whether the clinic is a 24-hour emergency hospital.
  • Whether treatment happens after hours, on weekends, or during holidays.

Some clinics may also require a deposit before beginning treatment or hospitalization. For example, one Ontario animal hospital states that hospitalized patients require a deposit equal to the estimated fee for the first 24 hours of medical care and hospitalization. Another Ontario emergency hospital intake form states that admitted animals require a 75% deposit.

Policies vary by clinic, which is why it helps to ask before there is an emergency.

Signs your dog may need emergency care

If you are unsure whether your dog needs urgent care, call your regular veterinarian or the nearest emergency animal hospital for guidance. If symptoms appear severe or are getting worse, do not wait for an article to confirm what to do.

Warning signs that may require emergency care include:

  • Trouble breathing, choking, or blue or pale gums.
  • Collapse, extreme weakness, or inability to stand.
  • Seizures, especially repeated seizures or a seizure lasting several minutes.
  • Suspected poisoning, including chocolate, cannabis, xylitol, medications, cleaners, or toxic plants.
  • Severe injury, uncontrolled bleeding, deep wounds, or trauma such as being hit by a vehicle.
  • A swollen or bloated abdomen, especially with restlessness or unproductive retching.
  • Repeated vomiting or diarrhea, especially with blood, weakness, or dehydration.
  • Signs of severe pain, crying, sudden aggression, or inability to get comfortable.
  • Difficulty urinating or inability to urinate.
  • Heatstroke symptoms such as heavy panting, confusion, weakness, vomiting, or collapse.

This list is not complete. When in doubt, call an emergency vet clinic and describe what is happening.

What to do before you leave for the clinic

In many emergencies, calling ahead can save time. The clinic may give first-step instructions, confirm whether they are accepting emergency patients, or direct you to another hospital if they are at capacity.

Before you leave, if it is safe to do so:

  • Call the emergency clinic and describe your dog's symptoms clearly.
  • Ask whether you should come in immediately or follow specific instructions first.
  • Bring your dog's medications, supplements, and recent medical records if available.
  • Bring your pet insurance details if you have coverage.
  • Ask how estimates and deposits are handled.
  • Keep your dog calm, warm or cool as appropriate, and safely restrained during transport.

If your dog is unconscious, unable to breathe normally, bleeding heavily, or in immediate danger, prioritize getting professional help as quickly as possible.

How to prepare for emergency vet costs

Many responsible dog owners budget for food, grooming, vaccinations, toys, and routine vet visits. Fewer are prepared for a sudden emergency bill.

That is understandable. A dog can seem completely fine in the morning and need urgent care by evening. The challenge is that emergency clinics often need decisions quickly. If the estimate is $1,000, $2,500, or $5,000, you may have to make a decision while emotions are high.

A practical plan may include more than one layer.

Build a pet emergency fund

The simplest option is to set aside money specifically for pet emergencies. Even a small emergency fund can reduce stress when something unexpected happens.

A good starting goal is $500 to $1,000. A stronger target is $2,000 or more, especially for larger dogs, senior dogs, or breeds with known health risks. The benefit is control: no approval process, no claim paperwork, and no waiting. The challenge is that it takes time to build.

Understand pet insurance before your dog gets sick

Pet insurance can be helpful for major accidents, illnesses, surgeries, and unexpected health events. It works best when purchased early, before conditions develop.

The important thing to understand is that pet insurance may not work like instant payment at the clinic. In many cases, you pay the vet first and submit a claim for reimbursement afterward. Some clinics or insurers may offer direct billing in certain situations, but you should confirm that before relying on it.

Ask clinics about payment expectations

Before an emergency happens, identify the closest 24-hour emergency vet clinics near you and ask:

  • Do you require a deposit for hospitalization or treatment?
  • Do you provide written estimates before treatment when possible?
  • What payment methods do you accept?
  • Do you work with pet insurance direct billing?
  • What should I do if I am on my way with a serious emergency?

Saving this information in advance can save time when you are already stressed.

Think through different bill sizes

It may feel uncomfortable, but it helps to decide ahead of time how you would handle a $1,000, $2,500, or $5,000 estimate. That does not mean you are expecting the worst. It means you are reducing one layer of panic if something happens.

Emergency vet preparedness checklist

Take 20 minutes this week and create a simple emergency plan for your dog.

  • Save the phone number and address of two nearby emergency vet clinics.
  • Know the fastest route from your home.
  • Keep your dog's medical records accessible.
  • Write down your pet insurance details, if you have coverage.
  • Save your regular veterinarian's after-hours instructions.
  • Know who can drive or help if you are not home.
  • Decide how you would pay for a $1,000, $2,500, or $5,000 emergency.
  • Keep poison control or emergency toxin guidance information handy.

Make your dog's emergency plan today.
Save two nearby emergency vet clinics, review their hours and payment policies, and keep your dog's medical records somewhere easy to access.

Final thought: make the plan before you need it

Emergency vet care is emotional. It is stressful. And yes, it can be expensive.

But preparing ahead of time gives you more control. Know where to go. Know what questions to ask. Know your payment expectations. Keep important information easy to find.

Your dog deserves fast care when something goes wrong. You deserve to make that decision with clarity, not panic.

Sources and further reading

  • Animal Emergency and Specialty Hospital client intake form
  • Bloor Animal Hospital deposit policy FAQ

This article is for general educational purposes and is not a substitute for veterinary advice. If you think your dog may be experiencing an emergency, contact a veterinarian or emergency animal hospital immediately.

title: What Dog Breed Is Right for Me? Try Our Dog Breed Match Quiz
excerpt: Not sure what dog breed fits your home, activity level, family, and grooming needs? Use our Dog Breed Match Quiz to find a practical breed shortlist.
description: Not sure what dog breed fits your home, activity level, family, and grooming needs? Use our Dog Breed Match Quiz to find a practical breed shortlist.
body:
Choosing a dog breed is exciting, but it can also be hard to do well.

Most people start with breeds they already know: a Labrador Retriever they grew up with, a Golden Retriever from a neighbour, a French Bulldog they see downtown, or a Poodle mix recommended by a friend. That is a natural place to start, but it can leave out the questions that matter most once the dog is actually living in your home.

How much exercise can you provide every day? How much grooming are you comfortable with? Do you live in an apartment, townhouse, detached home, or rural property? Are allergies a concern? Do you have young children, other pets, or limited training experience?

Those questions are exactly why we built the LeashFree.ca Dog Breed Match Quiz.

The quiz helps you narrow your search by comparing your lifestyle and preferences with structured traits from our dog breed database. It is not meant to make the final decision for you. It is meant to give you a smarter starting point.

Why choosing a breed is harder than it looks

A dog breed is more than a look. Size, coat type, exercise needs, training style, temperament, and home fit can all affect daily life.

A breed that looks perfect online may need more activity than your schedule allows. A small dog may not automatically be the best apartment dog if it is highly vocal, anxious, or difficult to settle. A low-shedding dog may be a better fit for allergies, but may also need professional grooming. A very intelligent working breed may be wonderful for an experienced, active owner and frustrating for a first-time owner who wants a calmer companion.

That is why a good breed search should start with lifestyle fit, not just popularity.

What the Dog Breed Match Quiz looks at

The quiz asks 8 practical questions about how a dog would fit into your real life. The questions cover:

  • Home type: apartment, townhouse, house with yard, or rural property.
  • Daily activity: from short walks and indoor play to a very active sport or working lifestyle.
  • Preferred size: small, medium, large, extra large, or no preference.
  • Shedding and grooming tolerance: whether you prefer minimal shedding or are flexible if the breed is otherwise a strong fit.
  • Household profile: adults only, older kids, young kids, or other pets in the home.
  • Training experience: from first-time dog owner to experienced handler.
  • Allergy needs: whether hypoallergenic-leaning or lower-shedding traits are important.
  • Breed type preference: purebred, designer or mixed breeds, or no preference.

After you answer, the quiz ranks breeds from the database and shows a shortlist with match percentages, breed traits, practical reasons, and links to full breed profiles.

How the quiz helps narrow the search

The quiz is designed to reduce overwhelm. Instead of browsing hundreds of breed profiles from scratch, you get a ranked list based on the lifestyle details you entered.

For example, if you live in a condo, prefer moderate activity, and want a lower-shedding companion, the quiz will give more weight to breeds that are marked as stronger apartment fits, manageable in size, and better aligned with your shedding or allergy preferences.

If you have a rural property and want a high-energy dog for outdoor activity, the quiz can surface different matches. If you are a first-time owner, trainability has more influence. If you have young children, family friendliness matters more.

This makes the results more practical than a simple list of popular breeds.

Why results are a shortlist, not a final answer

Breed traits are useful, but individual dogs still vary. Age, breeder or rescue background, early socialization, health, training, temperament, and daily routine all matter.

Use the quiz results as a research path. Read the full breed profiles. Talk to reputable breeders, rescues, shelters, trainers, and veterinarians. If you are adopting, ask about the individual dog's history, comfort with children or pets, exercise needs, and behaviour in a home setting.

The best match is not just the breed that scores highest. It is the dog whose needs you can meet consistently.

What to consider before choosing any breed

Before you make a decision, compare your top matches across a few important areas.

Activity level

Be honest about your normal week, not your ideal week. Some dogs can adapt to occasional quiet days. Others need significant daily exercise and mental work to stay healthy and settled.

Space and routine

Apartment living can work well for many breeds, but it depends on exercise, barking, training, elevator routines, potty access, and how much time the dog spends alone. Our guide to dogs for apartment living in Canada is a useful follow-up if space is one of your main concerns.

Family fit

Families should think about age of children, supervision, noise, visitor traffic, and how much time adults can commit to training. For more examples, see our guide to dog breeds for Canadian families.

Shedding and allergies

No breed is a guaranteed allergy solution for every person, but shedding level and coat type can still matter. If allergies or cleaning load are major factors, compare the quiz results with our guide to low-shedding dog breeds.

Training experience

Some breeds are eager to please and forgiving for new owners. Others are intelligent but independent, intense, or better suited to experienced handlers. A breed that is easy for one household can be a poor fit for another if the daily structure is not there.

How to use your quiz results

Once your results appear, start with the top 6 matches. Open the breed profiles that interest you and compare exercise needs, grooming expectations, trainability, size, and household suitability.

If the first set does not feel broad enough, use the Show 6 More Matches button to reveal more options. You can also copy, email, or share your quiz results with another person. That is useful if your family is comparing options together or if you want to discuss the shortlist with a trainer, rescue, breeder, or veterinarian.

Then use the full dog breed directory to keep researching. The quiz gives direction, but the breed profiles give the details.

Who the quiz is built for

The Dog Breed Match Quiz is especially useful if you are:

  • Choosing your first dog and do not know where to start.
  • Comparing several popular breeds and want a more objective shortlist.
  • Moving into an apartment or smaller home and want a realistic fit.
  • Trying to balance family needs, allergies, grooming, and activity level.
  • Open to both purebred and designer or mixed-breed options.
  • Helping a partner, parent, or child understand why some breeds may be better fits than others.

Try the Dog Breed Match Quiz

If you are asking, what dog breed is right for me?, the best next step is to compare your lifestyle against real breed traits.

Take the Dog Breed Match Quiz and get a ranked shortlist based on your home, activity level, grooming tolerance, allergies, household, training experience, and breed preferences.

It only takes a few minutes, and it gives you a more focused way to start researching your future dog.

Dog Breed Match Quiz FAQ

Is the Dog Breed Match Quiz free?

Yes. The LeashFree.ca Dog Breed Match Quiz is free to use.

Does the quiz include apartment-friendly breeds?

Yes. The quiz weighs apartment friendliness together with size, activity level, and your selected home type. You can also read our guide to apartment-friendly dog breeds.

Can the quiz tell me the perfect breed?

No quiz can guarantee a perfect breed. The results are a research starting point, not a final decision. Individual dogs vary, and you should still review health, temperament, training, and adoption or breeder details.

Does the quiz include mixed breeds?

Yes. The breed database includes purebred, designer, and some mixed-breed profiles where structured data is available.

What should I do after taking the quiz?

Open the top breed profiles, compare practical needs, share the shortlist with anyone involved in the decision, and speak with reputable breeders, rescues, shelters, trainers, or veterinarians before choosing a dog.

title: Introducing the Dog Food Comparison Tool Canada
excerpt: Learn why LeashFree.ca built a dog food comparison tool for Canadian dog owners and how it compares label-based nutrition, ingredients, calories, and estimated cost.
description: Learn why LeashFree.ca built a dog food comparison tool for Canadian dog owners and how it compares label-based nutrition, ingredients, calories, and estimated cost.
body:
Choosing dog food should be easier.

For many dog owners, comparing dog food brands can quickly become overwhelming. One bag says "high protein." Another says "grain-free." Another looks more affordable until you compare the bag size, calorie density, and feeding amount.

That is why we built the LeashFree.ca Dog Food Comparison Tool.

Our new tool helps Canadian dog owners compare dog food products side by side using practical, label-based information like nutrition, ingredients, calories, package size, and estimated cost. It is not about telling you which food is "best." It is about helping you compare available information more clearly.

Why we built this tool

LeashFree.ca started as a directory for leash-free dog parks across Canada, but our mission has always been broader than helping dog owners find places to walk their dogs.

We want LeashFree.ca to become a practical resource for Canadian dog owners. That means supporting more of the everyday decisions that come with caring for a dog, including where to exercise, how to understand breed needs, how to compare food options, and how to make care decisions with more confidence.

Dog food is one of the biggest recurring expenses for dog owners, and it is also one of the hardest things to compare fairly. A $95 bag is not automatically more expensive than a $70 bag. It depends on package size, calories per kilogram, and how long the food actually lasts.

What the Dog Food Comparison Tool does

The tool lets you select 2 to 4 dog foods and compare them side by side.

It looks at key information such as brand, product name, food type, life stage, main protein sources, grain-free or grain-inclusive status, guaranteed analysis, dry-matter protein, dry-matter fat, calories, package size, listed price, cost per kilogram, cost per 1,000 calories, estimated daily feeding cost, first five ingredients, ingredient flags, Made in Canada claims, and source or price-check dates.

Instead of making subjective claims, the tool highlights clear, measurable differences. For example, it may show which selected food has the lowest estimated daily cost, highest dry-matter protein, lowest dry-matter fat, highest calorie density, or a clearly different ingredient flag such as chicken-free, pea-free, grain-free, or grain-inclusive.

Why cost per bag is not enough

The price on the bag does not tell the full story. Two foods can have very different bag sizes, calorie density, feeding amounts, cost per kilogram, and cost per calorie.

That means one food may look cheaper upfront but cost more over time. Our tool calculates estimated values such as cost per kilogram, cost per 1,000 calories, and estimated daily cost based on a selected dog calorie amount.

These calculations are estimates, but they help compare foods more fairly than price alone.

Why we use dry-matter nutrition

Dog food labels usually show nutrition on an "as-fed" basis. That means the nutrition values include moisture.

This can make it difficult to compare products fairly, especially when comparing foods with different moisture levels. Our tool calculates dry-matter values for key nutrients like protein, fat, and fibre where the data is available.

By showing both the label value and the dry-matter value, the comparison uses a more consistent approach.

Built for Canadian dog owners

This tool is built specifically with Canadian dog owners in mind. Many dog food comparison articles include products, prices, or retailers that may not be relevant in Canada.

Our dataset focuses on dog foods commonly available to Canadian shoppers, including Canadian brands, Canadian-made foods, major retail brands, puppy foods, adult foods, senior foods, large-breed foods, grain-free recipes, and grain-inclusive recipes.

We also include source and price-check information so users can understand where the data came from and when it was last reviewed.

Who this tool is built for

The Dog Food Comparison Tool is built for dog owners who want a clearer way to compare food options.

  • New dog owners: Compare common products in a structured way when the number of options feels overwhelming.
  • Budget-conscious dog owners: Compare estimated daily cost instead of relying only on the sticker price.
  • Owners comparing brands: Review foods from brands such as ACANA, ORIJEN, FirstMate, Open Farm, Purina Pro Plan, Royal Canin, Hill's Science Diet, Performatrin, and others.
  • Owners watching ingredients: Spot listed ingredients such as chicken, beef, wheat, corn, soy, peas, lentils, or potatoes.
  • Owners of puppies, seniors, or large-breed dogs: Compare formulas by life stage and product type.
  • Research-minded dog owners: Review structured nutrition, ingredient, calorie, and price data instead of relying only on marketing copy.

What this tool is not

The LeashFree.ca Dog Food Comparison Tool is not veterinary advice. It does not diagnose health issues, recommend a medical diet, claim that one food is the healthiest, or replace advice from your veterinarian.

Every dog is different. Age, breed, size, activity level, health history, sensitivities, and body condition can all affect what food may be appropriate.

If your dog has a health condition, digestive issue, allergy concern, weight issue, or special nutritional need, speak with your veterinarian before changing foods.

Why we highlight differences with clear rules

One of the most important decisions we made was to avoid opinion-based scoring. You will not see a "food score" or a ranking based on unclear criteria.

Instead, the tool highlights measurable differences using clear rules. A protein highlight only appears when the difference is meaningful. A cost highlight only appears when the selected food is clearly lower in cost. Ingredient highlights appear when one selected food clearly differs from the others. Missing or older price data is shown as something to check.

The comparison is based on the data available, not hidden opinions.

Why accuracy matters

Dog food data can be tricky. Ingredients can change. Prices can change. Retailers may list different bag sizes. Some brands provide more complete nutrition data than others.

That is why we built a data-quality process behind the tool. Each product includes structured fields for nutrition, calories, ingredients, price, package size, sources, and review dates. We also use validation checks to catch missing data, duplicate products, stale prices, and incomplete records before they appear publicly.

What is included today

The first version includes a growing dataset of dry dog foods available in Canada. Current brands include ACANA, ORIJEN, FirstMate, Open Farm, GO! Solutions, NOW Fresh, Nutrience, Canadian Naturals, Boréal, Purina ONE, Purina Pro Plan, Royal Canin, Hill's Science Diet, IAMS, Pedigree, Blue Buffalo, Performatrin, Nutro, Wellness, Eukanuba, and Beneful.

We started with dry dog food because it is one of the most common formats purchased by Canadian dog owners and is easier to compare consistently by package size, calories, and daily cost.

Over time, we may expand into other food types, such as wet food, freeze-dried food, fresh food, or raw food, once we can support those comparisons accurately.

Our long-term goal

Our goal is to make LeashFree.ca more than a dog park directory. We want it to become a practical dog ownership resource for Canadians.

The Dog Food Comparison Tool is one step in that direction. It gives dog owners a better way to compare food options using structured information instead of relying only on marketing claims, package design, or price tags.

As we continue improving the tool, we plan to add more Canadian-market dog foods, better filters, more life-stage comparisons, improved ingredient search, clearer price freshness indicators, helpful educational content, and possibly user-requested foods for future review.

Try the Dog Food Comparison Tool

Choosing dog food can feel complicated, but comparing it should not be.

The LeashFree.ca Dog Food Comparison Tool helps you review nutrition, ingredients, calories, and price in one place so you can make a more informed decision for your dog.

Compare dog foods available in Canada.
Open the Dog Food Comparison Tool and select 2 to 4 foods to see how they differ side by side.

name: How Many Calories Should My Dog Eat Per Day?
title: How Many Calories Should My Dog Eat Per Day?
seoTitle: How Many Calories Should My Dog Eat Per Day?
metaDescription: Learn how to estimate your dog's daily calorie needs using RER and MER, then use our dog calorie calculator to turn weight, activity, and life stage into a daily kcal target.
description: Learn how to estimate your dog's daily calorie needs using RER and MER, then use our dog calorie calculator to turn weight, activity, and life stage into a daily kcal target.
body:
Why Dog Calories Matter

Your dog's calorie needs affect more than body weight alone. The right amount helps support energy, muscle condition, digestion, mobility, and long-term health.

Too many calories over time can lead to weight gain and added stress on joints. Too few calories can leave a dog under-fuelled or nutritionally short if portions are cut too far.

The goal is not a perfect fixed number forever. The goal is a strong starting point, regular check-ins, and gradual adjustments based on body condition.

The Difference Between RER and MER

Most calorie estimates start with two key terms: RER and MER.

RER means Resting Energy Requirement. It estimates calories needed for basic body functions at rest.

Common formula: RER = 70 ? body weight in kg^0.75

MER means Maintenance Energy Requirement. It adjusts RER for real-life factors like activity level, life stage, neuter status, growth, and weight goals.

In simple terms: MER = RER ? life-stage or activity factor

That MER value is your estimated daily calorie target.

What Affects Your Dog's Daily Calorie Needs?

Two dogs with the same weight may need different calorie amounts. Needs can vary by age, activity level, ideal weight, body type, metabolism, health status, and lifestyle.

  • Age and life stage
  • Current and ideal weight
  • Activity level
  • Spay/neuter status
  • Breed and body composition
  • Medical conditions
  • Pregnancy or nursing
  • Climate and daily routine

For example, an active young dog may need far more calories than a sedentary senior of the same size. Puppies also need more calories per pound than most adults because they are still growing.

How to Use a Dog Calorie Calculator

To estimate your dog's calories, enter weight, life stage, activity level, and goal (maintain, lose, or gain). Our Dog Calorie Calculator then returns an estimated daily target in kcal/day.

Remember this target includes everything your dog eats in a day: meals, treats, chews, toppers, and training rewards.

How to Convert Calories Into Food Amount

Once you have a daily calorie target, use the calorie information on your dog food label:

  • kcal per cup
  • kcal per can
  • kcal per 100 g
  • kcal per kg

Then convert:

  • Cups/day = daily kcal target ? kcal per cup
  • Cans/day = daily kcal target ? kcal per can
  • Grams/day = daily kcal target ? kcal per gram

Example: if your dog needs 600 kcal/day and food provides 400 kcal/cup, then 600 ? 400 = 1.5 cups/day (0.75 cups per meal if feeding twice daily).

For better consistency, use a kitchen scale when possible.

Should Dogs Eat Once or Twice a Day?

Most adult dogs do well with two meals per day. Some do fine with one, while others do better with smaller, more frequent feedings.

Puppies usually need three to four smaller meals daily, especially at younger stages. Dogs with medical or digestive needs may require a custom schedule from a veterinarian.

How to Tell If the Calorie Target Is Working

A calculator gives a starting estimate, but body condition confirms whether intake is right.

  • Ribs should be easy to feel without being sharply visible
  • A visible waist should be present from above
  • A slight abdominal tuck should be visible from the side
  • Energy should remain steady

After portion changes, reassess after 1 to 2 weeks. If weight change is too fast, adjust by about 5 to 10 percent and reassess.

Can You Use a Dog Calorie Calculator for Weight Loss?

Yes, with care. If a dog is overweight, targets are often based on ideal weight rather than current weight. Weight loss should be gradual and nutritionally complete.

Avoid aggressive food cuts that can increase hunger and reduce nutrient intake. For significant weight loss, veterinary guidance is recommended.

Feeding by Calories vs Feeding by Cups

Calories are usually more accurate than cups because foods vary in energy density. A cup is volume, not nutrition.

Tracking by calories also helps account for treats. If your dog needs 700 kcal/day and gets 100 kcal from treats, meals should provide about 600 kcal that day.

Common Mistakes When Estimating Dog Calories

  • Forgetting to count treats and extras
  • Treating bag feeding guides as fixed rules
  • Not recalculating after lifestyle or life-stage changes
  • Making large feeding changes too quickly

When to Ask Your Veterinarian

A calculator is useful, but it does not replace veterinary care. Ask your veterinarian if your dog is a fast-growing puppy, pregnant, nursing, underweight, overweight, a senior with appetite changes, on a prescription diet, or showing unexpected weight change.

Calculate Your Dog's Daily Calories

Use our free Dog Calorie Calculator to estimate kcal/day from weight, activity level, and life stage.

Use the result as a starting point, monitor body condition, and adjust gradually over time.

FAQ

How many calories should my dog eat per day?

It depends on weight, age, activity, body condition, and health status. A calorie calculator using RER and MER is the easiest place to start.

What does kcal mean on dog food?

Kcal means kilocalories. On pet food labels, kcal is the same unit commonly called Calories.

Should I feed my dog based on calories or cups?

Calories are more accurate because cup volume can hide large differences in food density across brands and formulas.

Do treats count toward my dog's daily calories?

Yes. Treats, chews, toppers, scraps, and training rewards all count toward total daily intake.

How often should I recalculate my dog's calories?

Recalculate when weight, activity, life stage, health status, or diet changes. Recheck every few weeks during active weight management.

Can puppies use a dog calorie calculator?

Yes, but puppies have different growth needs. Use a puppy setting and consult your veterinarian, especially for large-breed puppies.

Not sure how many calories your dog needs?
Use our free Dog Calorie Calculator to estimate a daily kcal target based on weight, activity level, and life stage.

description: Why do dogs bury bones, tilt their heads, or eat grass? Discover the 15 most Googled dog questions - answered with fun, science-backed insights for Canadian dog owners.
body:
1. Why Do Dogs Bury Bones?

This behavior is an ancient instinct. DogsÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ wild ancestors often buried leftover food to save it for later - natureÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s version of a refrigerator!

Even though your Lab has a full bowl of kibble and sleeps on a cozy bed, those survival instincts linger. Modern dogs might bury toys, bones, or treats as a way to Ã¢â‚¬Å“storeÃ¢â‚¬Â their resources or simply because itÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s fun and comforting.

Ã°Å¸â€™Â¡ Tip: If your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s burying habit gets messy, offer them puzzle toys or a sandbox-style dig zone to redirect the behavior.

2. How Do I Introduce Dogs Safely?

Bringing home a new dog? Introductions can make or break first impressions.
HereÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s a safe step-by-step guide for smooth introductions:

  1. Meet in neutral territory (a quiet park or sidewalk).
  2. Keep both dogs leashed and calm - let them sniff from a distance.
  3. Watch body language - wagging tails and loose posture are good signs.
  4. Keep sessions short, positive, and treat-filled.
  5. Once comfortable, move to your yard or home for longer playtime.

Ã°Å¸â€˜â€° Related Reading: Dog Socialization Tips

3. How Do I Stop My Dog from Digging?

Regional Differences in Vet Costs

Urban areas like Toronto, Vancouver, and Calgary tend to charge 20Ã¢â‚¬â€œ40% more for veterinary care due to higher clinic overhead. In smaller cities or rural regions, fees are often lower, but specialty services (like imaging or oncology) may require referral to larger centres.

Why Costs Are Rising

  1. Advanced diagnostics - MRI and ultrasound now common in routine cases.
  2. Inflation and staffing shortages - veterinary wages and supply costs increased.
  3. Pet humanization trend - more owners pursue advanced treatments.
  4. Post-pandemic backlog - clinics expanded hours and emergency fees.

How Pet Insurance Helps Offset Costs

Without insurance, one emergency can derail a family budget. Most Canadian plans reimburse 70Ã¢â‚¬â€œ90% of eligible expenses after your deductible - helping you focus on care, not cost.

title: Best Greeting Exercises to Reduce Jumping, Barking, or Biting
seoTitle: Best Greeting Exercises to Stop Dog Jumping, Barking & Biting | LeashFree.ca
metaDescription: Discover the best greeting exercises to teach your dog calm, polite hellos. Learn how to stop jumping, barking, or nipping with positive, easy-to-follow training tips from LeashFree.ca.
description: Discover the best greeting exercises to teach your dog calm, polite hellos. Learn how to stop jumping, barking, or nipping with positive, easy-to-follow training tips from LeashFree.ca.
body:
Why Dogs Jump, Bark, or Nip During Greetings

Dogs greet with their whole bodies Ã¢â‚¬â€ itÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s how they express joy and excitement. But in human households, that enthusiasm can turn into behaviors like:

  • Jumping up to reach your face
  • Barking loudly from excitement or attention-seeking
  • Mouthing or nipping as part of play

Most of these actions come from overstimulation or inconsistent greetings. The goal isnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t to punish the behavior Ã¢â‚¬â€ itÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s to redirect it into calm, confident manners.

1. Teach the Ã¢â‚¬Å“Four on the FloorÃ¢â‚¬Â Rule

Start by reinforcing that good things only happen when all four paws stay on the ground.
How to practice:

  1. Step inside calmly and ignore any jumping or barking.
  2. The moment your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s paws touch the ground, reward with gentle praise or a treat.
  3. If they jump again, turn away and repeat.

Ã°Å¸Â¦Â´ Pro tip: Consistency is key Ã¢â‚¬â€ ensure every family member and guest follows the same rule.

2. Reward Calm Before Contact

Instead of greeting your dog the second you walk in, wait until they show calm body language.
Look for:

  • Relaxed tail and posture
  • Quiet mouth
  • Soft eyes

Once theyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re calm, kneel down to their level, then offer affection or a treat. This helps your dog associate calm behavior with positive attention.

3. Use a Designated Ã¢â‚¬Å“Greeting SpotÃ¢â‚¬Â

Create a routine where your dog sits in a specific area when someone enters the home Ã¢â‚¬â€ such as by the door or on a mat.
To teach:

  1. Guide them to their mat using a leash or treat.
  2. Say Ã¢â‚¬Å“placeÃ¢â‚¬Â or Ã¢â‚¬Å“spot.Ã¢â‚¬Â
  3. Reward them for staying as you open the door or say hello.

This builds impulse control and prevents crowding at the doorway Ã¢â‚¬â€ a major trigger for jumping and barking.

4. Practice Controlled Greetings with Friends

Invite calm, dog-savvy friends to help practice greetings in a controlled environment.

  1. Ask your friend to approach slowly.
  2. Cue your dog to sit or stay.
  3. If your dog remains calm, allow a brief greeting.
  4. If they jump or bark, have the person turn and walk away immediately.

Your dog quickly learns: calm = attention, chaos = no fun.

5. Try the Ã¢â‚¬Å“Sit for HelloÃ¢â‚¬Â Routine

Teach your dog that sitting earns them all the good stuff Ã¢â‚¬â€ attention, play, and love.

  • Before greeting, ask for a sit.
  • Once they hold the sit for a few seconds, offer gentle pets and praise.
  • Over time, this becomes automatic whenever they see people approaching.

This simple exercise replaces jumping with a calm, polite behavior that works in any setting Ã¢â‚¬â€ at home, on walks, or at the dog park.

6. Redirect Excess Energy Before Greetings

Sometimes excitement is just too high to manage.
Try taking your dog for a quick walk or sniff session before guests arrive. A few minutes of light exercise can:

  • Burn off pent-up energy
  • Lower adrenaline levels
  • Make training more effective

A tired dog is a well-behaved dog!

7. Avoid Punishment Ã¢â‚¬â€ Use Calm Leadership Instead

Yelling Ã¢â‚¬Å“No!Ã¢â‚¬Â or pushing your dog away can actually make the behavior worse by adding to the excitement or fear.
Instead:

  • Stay quiet and calm
  • Remove attention when bad behavior happens
  • Reward the moment they settle down

This teaches emotional control Ã¢â‚¬â€ the foundation for all good manners.

Bonus Tip: Practice Real-World Greetings on Walks

Use every walk as a training opportunity. When you meet a neighbour or another dog:

  1. Stop and cue a sit.
  2. Only allow the greeting if your dog stays calm.
  3. End the greeting if they jump or bark.

Over time, your dog learns that calm greetings lead to more social fun.

The Long-Term Goal: Calm Confidence in Every Interaction

With regular practice, your dog will learn that greetings donÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t have to be chaotic. TheyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ll start to approach every hello with confidence, self-control, and tail-wagging joy Ã¢â‚¬â€ without the jumping or barking frenzy.

Ã°Å¸ÂÂ¶ Final Thoughts

Remember: good greetings are taught, not natural.
Your dog simply needs clear rules, consistent cues, and lots of positive reinforcement. With daily practice and patience, those once-crazy welcomes will turn into the calm, loving moments you always hoped for.

Ã¢â‚¬Â

metaDescription: Discover the best hypoallergenic dog breeds for Canadian families. From Poodles to Schnauzers, explore low-shedding, allergy-friendly breeds perfect for family life.
description: Discover the best hypoallergenic dog breeds for Canadian families. From Poodles to Schnauzers, explore low-shedding, allergy-friendly breeds perfect for family life.
body:
Why Ã¢â‚¬Å“HypoallergenicÃ¢â‚¬Â DoesnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t Mean Ã¢â‚¬Å“Allergy-FreeÃ¢â‚¬Â

  • Dogs still produce dander, saliva proteins, and urine proteins, which can trigger allergies.
  • Hypoallergenic breeds typically have low-shedding coats or hair-like fur that traps dander.
  • Regular grooming and cleaning remain essential for allergy-sensitive homes.

Top Hypoallergenic Dog Breeds for Families in Canada

1. Poodle (Standard, Miniature, and Toy)

  • Why theyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re great: Highly intelligent, trainable, and adaptable in size.
  • Coat: Dense, curly coat that sheds minimally.
  • Family fit: Wonderful with children, versatile for both condos and houses.
  • Canadian lifestyle: Active enough for outdoor families, yet calm indoors.

2. Bichon Frise

  • Why theyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re great: Cheerful, affectionate, and playful without being overwhelming.
  • Coat: Soft, curly coat with minimal shedding.
  • Family fit: Perfect for families with young kids or seniors.
  • Canadian lifestyle: Small and adaptable, ideal for condos or urban living.

3. Portuguese Water Dog

  • Why theyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re great: Loyal, energetic, and loves swimmingÃ¢â‚¬â€perfect for Canadian summers.
  • Coat: Water-resistant curly coat, low-shedding.
  • Family fit: Excellent for active families who love the outdoors.
  • Fun fact: Famously chosen by the Obama family due to allergies.

4. Schnauzer (Miniature, Standard, and Giant)

  • Why theyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re great: Protective, intelligent, and family-oriented.
  • Coat: Wiry, double-layer coat with minimal shedding.
  • Family fit: Great watchdogs, loyal companions for kids.
  • Canadian lifestyle: Hardy and adaptable to different climates.

5. Maltese

  • Why theyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re great: Gentle, affectionate, and adaptable to smaller homes.
  • Coat: Long, silky hair with low dander.
  • Family fit: Ideal for families seeking a lapdog with low-shedding needs.
  • Canadian lifestyle: Compact size makes them perfect for city living.

6. Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier

  • Why theyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re great: Friendly, lively, and great with kids.
  • Coat: Wavy, single-layer coat that produces less dander.
  • Family fit: A playful, medium-sized breed for active households.
  • Canadian lifestyle: Enjoys outdoor activity but not overly demanding.

7. Lagotto Romagnolo

  • Why theyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re great: Affectionate, eager to please, and a rare but growing favorite.
  • Coat: Dense, curly coat similar to a Poodle.
  • Family fit: Gentle and adaptable, bonds closely with family members.
  • Canadian lifestyle: Great for active families, especially those who enjoy outdoor adventures.

Tips for Allergy-Sensitive Families

  • Grooming: Regular brushing and professional grooming to manage dander.
  • Cleaning: HEPA filters and frequent vacuuming help reduce allergens.
  • Bathing: Weekly baths with dog-safe shampoo can minimize dander.
  • Trial period: Spend time with the breed before adopting to test sensitivity.

Conclusion

For Canadian families managing allergies, choosing the right dog breed makes all the difference. From the versatile Poodle to the playful Bichon Frise, these hypoallergenic breeds offer companionship without as many allergy triggers. With the right grooming routine and a little planning, you can enjoy the joy of dog ownership allergy-free.

name: Crate Training 101
title: Crate Training 101: How to Make Crate Time Positive for Your Puppy
seoTitle: Crate Training 101: Positive Puppy Training Guide | LeashFree.ca
metaDescription: Learn how to crate train your puppy the positive way. Step-by-step tips for Canadian families to make crate time safe, comfortable, and stress-free.
description: Learn how to crate train your puppy the positive way. Step-by-step tips for Canadian families to make crate time safe, comfortable, and stress-free.
body:
Why Crate Training Matters

  • Provides a safe space: Dogs instinctively seek out dens.
  • Helps with house training: Puppies learn bladder control more quickly.
  • Reduces separation anxiety: Builds independence in small increments.
  • Safety: Prevents destructive chewing or accidents when unsupervised.

Read our Separation Anxiety Guide for more on helping your dog feel calm when left alone.

Step 1: Choose the Right Crate

  • Size matters: Your puppy should be able to stand, turn, and lie comfortablyÃ¢â‚¬â€no bigger.
  • Types of crates: Wire, plastic, or soft-sided. Wire crates with dividers grow with your puppy.
  • Location: Place the crate in a quiet corner of the living room or bedroom, not in isolation.

Step 2: Introduce the Crate Slowly

  • Leave the crate door open with a cozy blanket or crate pad.
  • Toss treats or toys inside so your puppy chooses to explore.
  • Feed meals inside the crate to create positive associations.

Step 3: Short, Positive Sessions

  • Start with just a few minutes while youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re nearby.
  • Gradually increase crate time in small increments.
  • Never force your puppy insideÃ¢â‚¬â€patience is key.

Step 4: Use the Crate for Rest, Not Punishment

  • The crate should never be a Ã¢â‚¬Å“time-out zone.Ã¢â‚¬Â
  • Encourage naps in the crate with a chew toy or stuffed Kong.
  • Over time, your pup will retreat there voluntarily for comfort.

Step 5: Nighttime and Alone Time Training

  • Puppies may whine initiallyÃ¢â‚¬â€ignore mild protest unless it signals real need.
  • Place the crate near your bed at first to reassure them.
  • Slowly move it farther away as independence builds.

Step 6: Troubleshooting Common Issues

  • Whining or barking: Increase exercise and enrichment; donÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t reward whining with release.
  • Accidents in the crate: Ensure the crate isnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t too big and follow regular potty schedules.
  • Fearful puppy: Go back to basicsÃ¢â‚¬â€treats, short sessions, and no pressure.

Canadian Considerations

  • Cold winters: Line the crate with insulated pads or covers for warmth.
  • Small-space living: Collapsible crates work well in condos or apartments.
  • Travel: Crate training makes road trips and air travel easier.

Conclusion

Crate training, when done with patience and positivity, creates a safe, secure, and happy space for your puppy. It helps with house training, reduces anxiety, and builds good habits that last a lifetime.

Turn your dog into a pumpkin using an old orange T-shirt and green felt.

  • Use soft white gauze or strips from an old bedsheet.

  • Secure with safety pins (out of reach).
    Safety tip: DonÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t wrap too tight Ã¢â‚¬â€ your pup should move freely.

Fast, fun, and full of flair!

  • Cut a small cape shape from fabric or an old pillowcase.
  • Attach using Velcro or ribbon around the collar area.
  • Add your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s initial or logo cut from felt.
    Best for: Active dogs like Labrador Retrievers or Border Collies.

Perfect for dogs who hate wearing clothes.
How to:

  • Cut a large heart shape from red cardboard.
  • Write Ã¢â‚¬Å“tyÃ¢â‚¬Â in white marker.
  • Punch a hole and attach to the collar with string or a clip.

Yeehaw! A small cowboy hat and a bandana make an instant hit.
How to:

  • Use a small stuffed animal cowboy hat or craft one from cardboard and felt.
  • Tie a Halloween-themed bandana around the neck.
    Photo-ready: Great for rustic fall photo sessions among pumpkins!

Give your dog wings Ã¢â‚¬â€ safely.
How to:

  • Cut soft foam or felt wings and attach them to a harness (never directly to your dog).
  • Add a small reflective strip for nighttime walks.
    Perfect for: Black-coated dogs like Miniature Pinschers.

7. Flower Garden Pup Ã°Å¸Å’Â¼

Turn your furry friend into a walking bouquet.
How to:

  • Use a green baby onesie or T-shirt as a base.
  • Glue artificial flowers around the neckline and back.
  • Optional: a soft felt butterfly on top for extra charm.

8. Chef Pup

Simple, cute, and hilarious!
How to:

  • Use a white baby T-shirt as a chef coat.
  • Add black felt Ã¢â‚¬Å“buttons.Ã¢â‚¬Â
  • Top with a mini paper chef hat secured gently with elastic.
    Great for: Friendly breeds like Golden Retrievers or Cocker Spaniels.

9. Ghost Dog

Classic and effortless.
How to:

  • Take a lightweight white sheet and cut holes for eyes and nose.
  • Use fabric-safe dye to add a subtle spooky pattern if youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢d like.

10. Matching DIY Duo

For pet parents who want to join the fun!
Ideas:

  • Dog as a donut Ã°Å¸ÂÂ©, owner as a coffee Ã¢Ëœâ€¢
  • Dog as a pirate Ã°Å¸ÂÂ´Ã¢â‚¬ÂÃ¢ËœÂ Ã¯Â¸Â, owner as a treasure chest Ã°Å¸â€™Â°

Safety Tips for DIY Dog Costumes

  • Always prioritize comfort Ã¢â‚¬â€ if your dog looks stressed, skip the costume.

name: Dealing with Separation Anxiety in Dogs
title: Dealing with Separation Anxiety in Dogs: A Family Guide That Works
seoTitle: Dealing with Dog Separation Anxiety: Proven Strategies | LeashFree.ca
metaDescription: Learn how to spot separation anxiety and use evidence-based training, environment tweaks, and pro tips to help your dog stay calm when youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re away.
description: Learn how to spot separation anxiety and use evidence-based training, environment tweaks, and pro tips to help your dog stay calm when youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re away.
body:
What separation anxiety looks like (and what it isnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t)

Common signs include: vocalizing (barking/howling), destructive chewing or scratching (often at exit points), pacing, panting, drooling, house soiling, and attempts to escape. These typically occur only when alone or when an attachment figure is absent. Hidden signs can be missed - use a simple pet cam to check what happens after you leave. Always rule out medical causes (GI upset, urinary issues, pain) with your vet.

Why it happens

Separation-related distress can be driven by anxiety, frustration, or loss of social guidance; triggers include changes to routine, rehoming, or history of limited alone-time practice (common after long holidays or remote-work periods).

The evidence-based core: desensitization + counterconditioning (DS/CC)

Research and clinical guidance consistently support gradual exposure to the trigger (being alone) at levels your dog can handle (no panic), paired with positive outcomes (calm, pleasant experiences). Increase difficulty slowly over sessions. Medication can be an adjunct early on to reduce arousal so learning can happen.

A step-by-step plan families can follow

Before you start (setup)

  • Veterinary checkup: rule out medical causes; ask if your dog might benefit from short-term meds while you train.
  • Baseline: film a normal Ã¢â‚¬Å“leavingÃ¢â‚¬Â to learn how quickly distress starts (e.g., within 1Ã¢â‚¬â€œ10 minutes).
  • Environment: pick a safe, consistent space (room or pen; crate only if your dog already relaxes there), add a comfy bed, water, and a long-lasting chew/puzzle.
  • Daily rhythm: exercise, potty, brief training, then rest before alone-time sessions to reduce pent-up energy.

Phase 1 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Decouple Ã¢â‚¬Å“departure cuesÃ¢â‚¬Â

Dogs learn your leaving routine: keys, shoes, coat. Randomize and practice each cue without leaving until itÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s boring (pick up keys Ã¢â€ â€™ sit down; put on coat Ã¢â€ â€™ make tea). Repeat short, calm reps across the day.

Phase 2 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Ã¢â‚¬Å“Micro-absencesÃ¢â‚¬Â (0Ã¢â‚¬â€œ60 seconds)

  • Start with door closes for 1Ã¢â‚¬â€œ5 seconds while you remain calm just outside. Return before stress escalates (use your cam).
  • Repeat 5Ã¢â‚¬â€œ10 reps; gradually increase to 10, 20, 30, 60 seconds over days.
  • Keep greetings and departures low-key (no big goodbyes).

Phase 3 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Build real-world durations

  • Progress in small jumps that your dog consistently handles without signs of distress (panting, whining, pacing). If signs appear, drop back to the last easy step and progress more slowly.

How this works

How the Dog Age Formula Works

The UCSD formula is based on molecular biology Ã¢â‚¬â€ specifically, how methyl groups accumulate on DNA over time. Dogs and humans both show predictable Ã¢â‚¬Å“epigenetic clocks,Ã¢â‚¬Â but dogsÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ clocks run much faster in the first few years of life.

Why Big Dogs Age Faster

One of the biggest mysteries in veterinary science is why large dogs have shorter lifespans. Current research suggests that rapid growth and higher metabolism lead to faster cell turnover and earlier aging.

5. How can I help my dog live longer?
Regular exercise, balanced nutrition, and annual checkups are key. Mental stimulation also promotes longevity.

title: Dog Insurance Waiting Periods Explained (Accident vs Illness)
seoTitle: Dog Insurance Waiting Periods Explained (Accident vs Illness)
metaDescription: Learn how dog insurance waiting periods work in Canada. Understand accident vs illness coverage, orthopedic conditions, and why enrolling early matters.
description: Learn how dog insurance waiting periods work in Canada. Understand accident vs illness coverage, orthopedic conditions, and why enrolling early matters.
body:
What Is a Dog Insurance Waiting Period?

A waiting period is the time between policy activation and when you can submit a claim for a new condition.

Even if your dog gets sick the day after you enroll, the insurer wonÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t cover it until the waiting period ends. This rule exists to stop Ã¢â‚¬Å“pre-existingÃ¢â‚¬Â issues from being claimed immediately after signup.

Typical Waiting Periods in Canada

Type of Coverage Typical Waiting Period Examples
Accidents 48 hours Ã¢â‚¬â€œ 5 days Broken bones, cuts, swallowed objects
Illnesses 14 Ã¢â‚¬â€œ 30 days Infections, digestive issues, allergies
Orthopedic Conditions 30 days Ã¢â‚¬â€œ 6 months Cruciate ligament tears, hip dysplasia
Alternative Therapies 14 Ã¢â‚¬â€œ 30 days Acupuncture, chiropractic care
Routine or Wellness Add-ons Varies May start immediately if offered

Each provider sets their own terms. For example:

  • Trupanion covers accidents and illnesses after 5 days and 30 days, respectively.
  • Pets Plus Us applies 48 hours for accidents and 14 days for illness.
  • Fetch by The Dodo uses a 15-day waiting period for both accident and illness.

Why Waiting Periods Exist

Waiting periods protect the insurance pool from adverse selection - people enrolling only after their dog gets injured or sick. Without them, costs would skyrocket for everyone.

Think of it like car insurance: you canÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t buy a policy after an accident and expect coverage for that incident.

How Waiting Periods Differ: Accident vs Illness

Accident Coverage

Accident waiting periods are short - usually 48 hours to five days. These cover sudden injuries such as:

  • Getting hit by a car
  • Broken limbs
  • Bite wounds or lacerations
  • Foreign object ingestion

Because accidents are random and not predictable, insurers keep this waiting period brief.

Illness Coverage

Illness waiting periods are longer (two to four weeks). They cover non-emergency health issues like:

  • Ear infections
  • Gastrointestinal issues
  • Skin allergies
  • Urinary tract infections

These longer periods prevent people from enrolling after noticing early signs of sickness.

Special Cases: Orthopedic and Hereditary Conditions

Some breeds are prone to orthopedic or hereditary issues, such as hip dysplasia or cruciate ligament tears.
Providers often require:

  • Extended waiting periods (up to 6 months) for orthopedic issues, or
  • Optional waiver forms signed by your vet confirming your dog is healthy

If you have a large or active breed (Labrador, German Shepherd, Golden Retriever), review this section carefully before choosing a plan.

Can Waiting Periods Be Waived?

In most cases, no. However:

  • Some providers will waive the orthopedic waiting period if your vet performs a healthy joint exam soon after enrollment.
  • Accident waiting periods sometimes begin immediately for policy renewals.

Always check your policy documents for Ã¢â‚¬Å“waiverÃ¢â‚¬Â language or Ã¢â‚¬Å“pre-enrollment exam requirements.Ã¢â‚¬Â

What Happens If Your Dog Gets Sick During the Waiting Period

If your dog shows symptoms during the waiting period, that condition becomes pre-existing and is excluded from future coverage.

Example:

  • You buy a plan on April 1.
  • Illness waiting period = 14 days.
  • Your dog develops vomiting on April 10.
    That condition and anything related to it will likely be considered pre-existing - even after the 14-day period ends.

Tips for New Policyholders

Ã¢Å“â€¦ Enroll early. The sooner you buy coverage, the sooner protection starts.
Ã¢Å“â€¦ Read the fine print. Each provider defines Ã¢â‚¬Å“waiting periodÃ¢â‚¬Â differently for accident, illness, and add-on coverage.
Ã¢Å“â€¦ Get a vet exam before enrolling. This can help confirm pre-existing status and sometimes shorten orthopedic waiting periods.
Ã¢Å“â€¦ Set expectations. DonÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t plan to use the insurance during the first few weeks for new issues.

Example Comparison: Trupanion vs Pets Plus Us

Provider Accident Waiting Period Illness Waiting Period Orthopedic Conditions
Trupanion 5 days 30 days 30 days
Pets Plus Us 48 hours 14 days 6 months (waiver possible)
Fetch by The Dodo 15 days 15 days 6 months
OVMA Pet Insurance 48 hours 14 days 6 months
This table illustrates why comparing policies matters - shorter waiting periods mean faster access to protection.

The Bottom Line

Dog insurance waiting periods are short but critical to understand.

  • Accidents are covered within days.
  • Illnesses and orthopedic issues require patience before youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re protected.

The key is enrolling before anything happens - especially for puppies or newly adopted dogs - so no future health problems are considered pre-existing.

Ã°Å¸â€˜â€° Compare waiting periods across Canadian providers with our Dog Insurance Comparison Tool.

FAQs About Dog Insurance Waiting Periods

Why canÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t coverage start immediately?

Insurers need time to verify that your dog isnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t already ill, preventing unfair claims and keeping costs lower for all members.

Does each provider have the same waiting period?

No Ã¢â‚¬â€ each sets its own timeline. Always confirm your providerÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s policy for accident, illness, and orthopedic coverage.

Can I use insurance during the waiting period?

You can visit your vet, but any costs incurred wonÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t be eligible for reimbursement until the waiting period ends.

What happens if my dog has symptoms right after enrolling?

That issue becomes pre-existing and may be permanently excluded from coverage.

Sources

  • Canadian Veterinary Medical Association (CVMA)
  • Trupanion Canada Policy Details
  • Pets Plus Us Canada
  • Fetch by The Dodo Pet Insurance

description: Learn the doÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s and donÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ts of dog park etiquette in Canada. From recall training to cleanup rules, discover how to keep off-leash parks safe and fun for everyone.
body:
Dog parks are a cornerstone of CanadaÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s dog-friendly communities. They give pups the freedom to run, socialize, and burn off energy Ã¢â‚¬â€ while offering owners a chance to connect, too. But these shared spaces only work when everyone plays by the same rules. In this guide, weÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ll walk through the essentials of dog park etiquette in Canada, from preparing your dog at home to handling tricky situations in the park.

Why Dog Park Etiquette Matters

  • Keeps dogs safe and prevents injuries.
  • Builds trust among owners.
  • Protects parks from complaints and closures

Preparing Your Dog Before You Go

Checklist

  • Up-to-date vaccinations.
  • Strong recall skills Ã¢â‚¬â€ your dog should come when called.
  • Proper socialization Ã¢â‚¬â€ your pup should be comfortable around others.
  • Spay/neuter encouraged (unfixed dogs may spark fights).

DoÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s and DonÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ts at the Dog Park

The DoÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s:

  • Supervise your dog at all times.
  • Pick up after your dog immediately.
  • Respect size zones (large dog / small dog areas).
  • Bring water (not all parks provide it).

name: Halloween Safety Tips for Dogs
title: Halloween Safety Tips for Dogs: Keep Your Pup Calm and Safe
seoTitle: Halloween Safety Tips for Dogs: Keep Your Pup Calm and Safe | LeashFree.ca
metaDescription: Keep your dog safe and stress-free this Halloween. Discover safety tips for costumes, candy, and trick-or-treat chaos tailored for Canadian pups.
description: Keep your dog safe and stress-free this Halloween. Discover safety tips for costumes, candy, and trick-or-treat chaos tailored for Canadian pups.
body:
1. Keep Candy Out of PawÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s Reach

Chocolate, xylitol, raisins, and many candies are toxic to dogs. Even small amounts can lead to vomiting, diarrhea, or worse.

  • Store all Halloween candy well above your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s reach.
  • Remind guests and kids not to share human treats.
  • Keep an emergency vet number handy - just in case.

2. Watch the Door Ã¢â‚¬â€ and the Disguises

Trick-or-treaters can be scary for dogs. Constant doorbell rings, strange smells, and costumed visitors can trigger stress or anxiety.

  • Keep your dog in a quiet, secure room away from the front door.
  • Play calming music or white noise to muffle sounds.
  • If your dog loves to greet guests, use a leash or baby gate for control.
Related: Read our post on Helping Dogs with Separation Anxiety for additional calming strategies.

3. Costumes: Comfort Before Cute

Dog costumes are adorable Ã¢â‚¬â€ but not every pup enjoys dressing up.

  • Always try the costume on days before Halloween.
  • Avoid anything tight, restrictive, or covering the eyes.
  • Choose breathable fabrics and ensure your dog can move freely.
  • Add reflective elements if youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ll be outdoors after dark.

4. Keep Decorations Dog-Safe

Halloween decorations can be just as hazardous as candy.

  • Keep candles, fake cobwebs, and cords out of reach.
  • Avoid decorations with dangling parts your dog could chew.
  • Use battery-operated lights instead of open flames.

5. Provide a Calm, Familiar Space

Even well-adjusted dogs can get overwhelmed by all the excitement.

  • Set up a Ã¢â‚¬Å“quiet zoneÃ¢â‚¬Â with their bed, toys, and water bowl.
  • Add calming scents like lavender or use a pheromone diffuser.
  • Reward calm behavior with treats and praise.

6. Identification and Safety Essentials

If your dog gets spooked and bolts out the door, proper ID can make all the difference.

  • Ensure your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s tags and microchip info are up to date.
  • Keep your dog leashed when opening the door.
  • Consider using a reflective collar or harness for evening walks.

7. Dog-Friendly Alternatives

If your dog loves being part of the celebration, find safe ways to include them:

  • Attend a local dog park Halloween meetup (check our Dog Parks Directory for events near you).
  • Host a calm Ã¢â‚¬Å“dog costume photo dayÃ¢â‚¬Â with friends.
  • Treat your pup to a homemade pumpkin dog biscuit instead of candy.

Conclusion

Halloween should be fun for everyone - including your dog. With a little extra care, you can enjoy the festivities while keeping your furry friend safe, calm, and happy.

Remember, not every pup loves the noise and excitement of Halloween - and thatÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s okay. Celebrate in ways that make them comfortable, and youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ll both have a tail-wagging good time.

seoTitle: How Cold Is Too Cold for a Dog Walk? | Winter Safety Guide for Canadian Dogs
metaDescription: Learn how cold is too cold for a dog walk with our vet-backed Canadian winter guide. Discover safe temperature limits, breed-specific tips, and cold-weather care advice to protect your pup this season.
description: Learn how cold is too cold for a dog walk with our vet-backed Canadian winter guide. Discover safe temperature limits, breed-specific tips, and cold-weather care advice to protect your pup this season.
body:
Understanding Dog Cold Tolerance

Every dog has a different threshold for the cold, depending on factors like size, coat type, body fat, and age. As a general rule:

  • Small and short-haired breeds (like Beagles or Weimaraners) feel the cold quickly.
  • Medium-coated breeds (like Golden Retrievers or Labradors) can tolerate short outdoor time in moderate cold.
  • Cold-weather breeds (like Huskies or Samoyeds) are built for subzero temperatures - but still have limits.

Below is a quick reference chart to help you gauge when itÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s safe to head out:

(Beagle, Weimaraner, Dachshund)		 Above -5Ã‚Â°C Ã¢Å“â€¦ Safe for normal walks
Medium Coat Breeds

Cold-Weather Breeds
(Siberian Husky, Samoyed, Newfoundland)		 -10Ã‚Â°C to -20Ã‚Â°C Ã¢Å“â€¦ Usually comfortable, monitor for frostbite
All Breeds Below -20Ã‚Â°C Ã°Å¸Å¡Â« Too cold Ã¢â‚¬â€ risk of frostbite & hypothermia

Signs Your Dog Is Too Cold

Even the fluffiest dogs have limits. Watch for these warning signs that itÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s time to head home:

  • Shivering or trembling
  • Whining or refusing to walk
  • Lifting paws off the ground
  • Hunched posture or tucked tail
  • Ice forming between paw pads or on whiskers

If your dog shows these signs, warm them up immediately indoors.

Tips for Safe Winter Walks

A few smart adjustments can make winter walks safe and enjoyable:

  • Dress appropriately: Short-haired or senior dogs benefit from a snug, insulated jacket.
  • Use dog booties or paw balm: Prevent frostbite and protect from salt or ice melt chemicals.
  • Time it right: Midday offers the warmest temperatures and brightest light.
  • Keep it short: In extreme cold, aim for 10Ã¢â‚¬â€œ15 minutes max, then continue playtime indoors.
  • Dry thoroughly: Always towel off paws and belly to avoid skin irritation.

Ã°Å¸ÂÂ¾ Breed-Specific Cold Tolerance

Some dogs are born for snow - others, not so much. Learn about your breedÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s comfort level:

  • Siberian Husky - thrives in frigid weather.
  • Golden Retriever - moderate cold tolerance, loves the snow.
  • Labrador Retriever - water-resistant coat but needs protection in long exposure.
  • Weimaraner - short coat, needs gear in cold climates.

Ã°Å¸Å’Â¬Ã¯Â¸Â Temperature Safety Quick Reference

Temperature (Ã‚Â°C) Activity Recommendation
0Ã‚Â°C to -5Ã‚Â°C Safe for most breeds, monitor small dogs.
-6Ã‚Â°C to -15Ã‚Â°C Limit walks to 15Ã¢â‚¬â€œ20 minutes. Use jackets or booties.
-16Ã‚Â°C to -25Ã‚Â°C Only short potty breaks. Avoid long exposure.
Below -25Ã‚Â°C Danger zone Ã¢â‚¬â€ stay indoors, switch to indoor play.

When ItÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s Too Cold to Go Out

If the temperature dips below your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s comfort zone, skip the walk and opt for mental and physical stimulation at home.
Try puzzle toys, indoor fetch, or even training refreshers to keep their mind active.

Ã¢â‚¬Â

Final Thoughts

When in doubt, trust your instincts. If youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re bundling up and still shivering, chances are your dog feels the same.
A few short walks combined with indoor enrichment will keep your furry friend both safe and satisfied during CanadaÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s chilliest months.

metaDescription: Learn how to choose the best dog park for your pup. Discover safety tips, size considerations, and Canadian-specific advice for leash-free adventures.
description: Learn how to choose the best dog park for your pup. Discover safety tips, size considerations, and Canadian-specific advice for leash-free adventures.
body:
Why Choosing the Right Dog Park Matters

  • Safety first: Not all parks have secure fencing or separate spaces for small dogs.
  • Socialization: Parks vary in how busy or structured they are, which can impact your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s comfort level.
  • Health: A clean, well-maintained park reduces the risk of illness or injury.
  • Lifestyle fit: Some dogs thrive in large open spaces, while others prefer quiet, smaller areas.

Read our Dog Park Etiquette Guide for tips on being a responsible owner.

1. Location & Accessibility

  • Proximity: Choose a park close enough for regular visits.
  • Parking & transit: Check if thereÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s parking or public transit access.
  • Canadian winters: Some parks are open year-round, while others may close in heavy snow.

2. Safety Features

  • Fencing: Secure, tall fences are essential for escape artists.
  • Gates: Double-gated entries prevent dogs from slipping out.
  • Surfaces: Look for grass, gravel, or mulchÃ¢â‚¬â€not broken glass or hazardous debris.

3. Size & Space

  • Small dogs: They may feel safer in smaller, designated areas.
  • Active breeds: Larger parks are ideal for Border Collies, Labrador Retrievers, or Australian Shepherds.
  • Shy dogs: Quiet parks with fewer visitors are best for gradual socialization.

4. Cleanliness & Maintenance

  • Waste disposal: Dog waste stations should be well-stocked with bags and bins.
  • General upkeep: Check if the grass is maintained and if trash is removed regularly.
  • Water sources: Access to clean drinking water is a big plus.

5. Community & Rules

  • Posted rules: A good park will have clear signage about leash-free areas, hours, and etiquette.
  • Community feel: Parks with engaged owners often feel safer and more enjoyable.
  • Local bylaws: Some cities have breed-specific or licensing rules to follow.

6. Trial Visits: Test the Fit

  • Visit at different times of day to see how busy the park gets.
  • Observe other dogs and ownersÃ¢â‚¬â€are they respectful, or is it chaotic?
  • Watch how your dog reacts: relaxed body language = good fit.

Canadian Dog Park Extras

  • Provincial parks: Some provincial parks in Ontario and BC offer large off-leash areas.
  • Urban parks: Toronto, Vancouver, and Calgary all have extensive dog park networks.
  • Winter readiness: Choose parks with cleared pathways during snowy months.

Conclusion

The right dog park can provide exercise, enrichment, and socialization, but the wrong one may overwhelm or endanger your pup. By considering safety, size, community, and cleanliness, you can find a park that fits your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s needs and your lifestyle.

Explore our Dog Park Directory to find leash-free spaces across Canada, from city parks to provincial trails.

name: How to Condo Train Your Puppy
title: How to Potty Train (House Train) Your Puppy in a Condo or Apartment
seoTitle: How to Potty Train (House Train) Your Puppy in a Condo or Apartment | LeashFree.ca
metaDescription: Learn how to potty train (house train) your puppy in a condo or apartment. Discover proven routines, tools, and Canadian-specific tips for successful urban training.
description: Learn how to potty train (house train) your puppy in a condo or apartment. Discover proven routines, tools, and Canadian-specific tips for successful urban training.
body:
Why Condo Potty Training is Different

  • Limited outdoor access: No backyard = scheduled elevator rides.
  • Weather challenges: Harsh Canadian winters can make outdoor breaks difficult.
  • Shared spaces: Hallways, lobbies, and elevators can distract or overstimulate puppies.

Step 1: Establish a Consistent Routine

  • Take your puppy out first thing in the morning, after meals, naps, and playtime.
  • Stick to set times so your puppy builds bladder control and expectations.
  • Use an indoor bell or cue word to signal Ã¢â‚¬Å“time to go.Ã¢â‚¬Â

Step 2: Choose the Right Spot

  • Outdoor option: Pick one consistent spot near your building.
  • Indoor option: Use a balcony turf mat, pee pads, or an indoor dog potty for backup.
  • Pro Tip: Avoid switching locations too often - it confuses your puppy.

Step 3: Reward and Reinforce

  • Always bring treats on potty trips.
  • Reward within 3 seconds of success so your puppy links action to reward.
  • Use consistent praise phrases like Ã¢â‚¬Å“Good potty!Ã¢â‚¬Â.

Step 4: Manage Accidents Calmly

  • Never punish or rub your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s nose - this creates fear.
  • Clean accidents thoroughly with enzyme cleaner to remove scent markers.
  • Reflect on timing: did you miss a cue or delay a trip outside?

Step 5: Overcome Common Condo Challenges

  • Elevator delays: Carry your puppy outside until theyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re old enough to wait.
  • Winter walks: Keep potty breaks short with jackets/booties.
  • Nighttime needs: Consider a nearby pee pad station for young puppies.

Tools That Help Condo Training

  • Puppy pee pads (starter stage only).
  • Turf patches/indoor potty systems for balconies.
  • Portable carriers for quick outdoor trips.
  • Training bells to teach puppies to signal.

Canadian Puppy Owner Tips

  • Plan for long winters -have an indoor backup solution.
  • Use dog-safe de-icer near building entrances to protect paws.
  • Socialize your puppy to elevators, lobbies, and shared areas during potty breaks.

Conclusion

House training your puppy in a condo or apartment takes extra patience and consistency, but itÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s absolutely possible. By establishing a solid routine, rewarding success, and preparing for CanadaÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s unique climate, youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ll set your puppy up for success in no time.

name: How to Help a Reactive Dog Stay Calm on Walks
title: How to Help a Reactive Dog Stay Calm on Walks
seoTitle: How to Help a Reactive Dog Stay Calm on Walks | LeashFree.ca
metaDescription: Walking a reactive dog can be stressful. Learn how to manage leash reactivity, reduce anxiety, and rebuild calm, confident walks through positive training.
description: Walking a reactive dog can be stressful. Learn how to manage leash reactivity, reduce anxiety, and rebuild calm, confident walks through positive training.
body:
Recognizing the Signs of Reactivity

Before addressing the behavior, learn to spot early warning signals. A reactive dog might:

  • Stiffen their body or raise hackles
  • Stare intently or Ã¢â‚¬Å“lock onÃ¢â‚¬Â to a target
  • Lunge or bark suddenly
  • Growl, whine, or pace

Catching these signals early allows you to redirect your dog before a full reaction occurs.

Why Reactivity Happens on Leash

Leash reactivity is especially common. When restrained, dogs canÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t create space - their natural coping strategy. This loss of control builds frustration, leading to lunging or barking.

Dogs also sense tension in your leash grip or body language. The more you tighten up, the more they believe something is wrong.
ThatÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s why reactivity training often starts with relaxation - for both of you.

How to Help a Reactive Dog Stay Calm

1. Identify and Manage Triggers

Keep a simple journal for a week: note when your dog reacts, what the trigger was, and how close it was.
Patterns will emerge Ã¢â‚¬â€ maybe your dog reacts only to other dogs on narrow sidewalks, or men wearing hats.

Once you know the triggers, you can adjust distance or route to avoid overwhelming situations.

2. Practice Threshold Training

Your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s threshold is the point where they notice a trigger but can still focus on you.
Stay under that threshold and reward calm behavior with treats or praise.
Gradually reduce distance over multiple sessions as your dog gains confidence.

This method - called desensitization and counter-conditioning - replaces fear with positive associations.

3. Reward Calm, Not Reactivity

When your dog looks at a trigger without reacting, calmly mark and reward:
Ã¢â‚¬Å“Good job!Ã¢â‚¬Â Ã¢â€ â€™ treat.
This teaches them that staying composed earns rewards, while lunging doesnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t.

Use high-value treats (like chicken or cheese) that your dog only gets during training walks.

4. Create Distance and Safety

If your dog begins to react, move away calmly. Avoid yanking the leash or shouting.
Walk in a gentle arc, keeping your tone upbeat Ã¢â‚¬â€ think Ã¢â‚¬Å“LetÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s go this way!Ã¢â‚¬Â
Distance reduces stress and resets focus faster than correction.

5. Train Focus Cues

Teach your dog a reliable Ã¢â‚¬Å“look at meÃ¢â‚¬Â or Ã¢â‚¬Å“leave itÃ¢â‚¬Â cue at home first.
Then use it on walks to redirect attention from triggers.
Reward eye contact and relaxation. Over time, your dog learns to check in with you automatically when unsure.

6. Use the Right Equipment

Avoid retractable leashes or tight collars - they can increase tension.
Opt for:

  • A well-fitted front-clip harness
  • A 6-foot leash for control without pressure
  • A treat pouch for quick rewards

In high-traffic areas, bring a lightweight barrier item (like your body or a car) to create quick visual space between your dog and triggers.

7. Stay Consistent and Patient

Progress with reactive dogs happens in small steps - not overnight.
Celebrate small victories, like calmly watching another dog across the street.
Avoid high-pressure situations until your dog has built reliable calm responses.

When to Seek Professional Help

If your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s reactions are intense, unpredictable, or difficult to manage, work with a certified force-free trainer or behavior consultant.
Professionals can help you design a gradual desensitization plan that keeps your dog below threshold while rebuilding confidence.

Look for trainers certified through CCPDT or IAABC, and avoid those using punishment or aversive tools.

Real-World Canadian Tips

Cold weather can make walks more challenging for reactive dogs - limited daylight, bulky clothing, and icy footing add stress.
Try these adaptations:

  • Shorter, more frequent walks in quiet neighborhoods
  • Using reflective gear and well-lit routes
  • Practicing Ã¢â‚¬Å“indoor socializationÃ¢â‚¬Â at pet stores or training facilities

Reactivity management is about building trust - not perfection.

Final Thoughts

Reactivity can feel discouraging, but itÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s truly manageable with consistency, empathy, and time.
Your goal isnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t to eliminate reactions entirely - itÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s to help your dog recover quickly and feel safe again.

Remember: calm behavior is learned through trust, not correction.
Each successful walk strengthens your dogÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s confidence - and your bond.

Common triggers include:

  • Other dogs or animals
  • Strangers or children
  • Loud noises (cars, bikes, skateboards)
  • Crowded environments

Reactivity often stems from fear, frustration, or lack of early socialization. The good news? With patience and consistent training, most dogs can learn to stay calm, even around their triggers.

Recognizing the Signs of Reactivity

Before addressing the behavior, learn to spot early warning signals. A reactive dog might:

  • Stiffen their body or raise hackles
  • Stare intently or Ã¢â‚¬Å“lock onÃ¢â‚¬Â to a target
  • Lunge or bark suddenly
  • Growl, whine, or pace

Catching these signals early allows you to redirect your dog before a full reaction occurs.

Why Reactivity Happens on Leash

Leash reactivity is especially common. When restrained, dogs canÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t create space - their natural coping strategy. This loss of control builds frustration, leading to lunging or barking.

Dogs also sense tension in your leash grip or body language. The more you tighten up, the more they believe something is wrong.
ThatÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s why reactivity training often starts with relaxation - for both of you.
